speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in accordance with our practice I wish to report to the house on the NATO ministerial meeting which took place this week in Brussels. Also in accordance with practice in other years and with the consent of the house I should like to table two copies in French and two copies in English of the final communique of this meeting; and if the house agrees, as it has on other occasions, I suggest that this be published as an appendix to today's Hansard.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NATO-REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext: Is that agreed?

subtopic: NATO-REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MEETING

Agreed.
[Editor's note: For text of communique referred to above, see appendix.]

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NATO-REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
The discussions at this meeting covered a wide range of problems, but our attention was necessarily concentrated on issues directly related to the French decision, while remaining within the alliance, to withdraw from the integrated military structure.
The nature of the main problems that we had to discuss, which were internal to the alliance, made necessary an unprecedented organization of work. The meetings on Monday, June 6, were among the foreign ministers of the 14 countries, to which the government of France had sent communications. It also proved necessary in the case of the regular ministerial meetings for the 14 ministers to hold meetings several times separately in order to work out among themselves a common position on issues under negotiation with the French. This too was an unprecedented procedural development and one which could have created difficulty. That it worked smoothly I regard as evidence of the good will of all members of the alliance. I am also encouraged to think that it reflected their genuine desire to develop forms of relationships which would make possible continuing co-operation in the future.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
Never in my experience has there been a NATO meeting where the exchanges were franker, and perhaps where the problems were more difficult. This was hardly surprising. Ministers found when they reached Brussels that both among the 14 and as between the 14 and France they were divided on two important questions: the 14 had differing and strongly held views as to whether a new site should be chosen for the North Atlantic council, and previous efforts to find a formula to cover negotiations between France and the 14 over the future role of French forces in Germany had proved abortive.
These two issues of the meetings-the site of the NATO council and the negotiating procedures for French forces in Germany-involved for us a common concern. At stake in each case was the continued unity of the alliance. We avoided open breaches. Orderly procedures for examining our differences were agreed upon. Time was gained. I do not deny that we have difficult problems ahead of us. The 14 proved to themselves that they could hold to a common position, and France found that its allies were ready to compromise in order to preserve the unity of the alliance.
Now, sir, reporting on these very vital meetings, I do not want to give an exaggerated impression of the achievements of the meeting. In concrete terms we succeeded in working out a procedure for conducting negotiations on the several problems involving all members of the alliance which are posed by the French decision to withdraw from the integrated military structure. Moreover, the intensive and delicate discussions which led up to this agreement, and which lasted for two days, were marked by efforts on both sides to resist any formula which they considered might prejudice their position in the negotiations which would ensue. This confirmed what we already knew, that it will prove extremely difficult to find a way to reconcile at the same time the requirement of the 14 that French forces remaining in Germany should undertake a

June 10, 1966
External Affairs
militarily significant role, with French insistence on the principle that their forces should not be integrated.
The question at issue here is the extent of the military co-operation which the French government will be prepared to provide as a substitute for participation in the integrated military structure; for it is necessary to have a concerted planning in peace time if there is to be effective response in emergencies and concerted action in war. The outcome of these complex and crucial negotiations cannot be forecast, but they are at least fairly launched.
The other issue faced at Brussels concerned the future site of the North Atlantic council. This was the main issue which divided the 14. There were some who felt keenly that a decision had to be taken immediately to move the council from Paris. With SHAPE, the military headquarters, obliged to leave French territory, they argued the case for the co-location of the military and civil headquarters.
A decision to move the council from Paris would be an important political action. I argued; would it have been right to have taken such a step before testing French intentions; before discovering whether co-operative military arrangements could be worked out between the French and the 14 who have decided to maintain the integrated military structure; even before President de Gaulle had visited Moscow, even before the French foreign minister had reached Brussels and had a chance to show, in consultation with his colleagues, whether satisfactory arrangements could be worked out with France? How could we hope to work out such arrangements with France, the Canadian delegation argued, if our first action as the 14 was to anticipate that our negotiations with the French would fail?
These are the questions I put to my colleagues. No matter how valid some of the arguments for moving the council might be, we maintained it was too early to take a decision. Eventually, after the fullest discussion, the 14 ministers agreed to defer consideration of the question until October.
The French foreign minister later spoke in the ministerial meeting of the position taken by the 14. He said the French government would be pleased if the 14 decided that the council should remain in Paris, but if it were decided to move the council, France would understand the reasons. This statement, which is noted in the communique,

helped to clear the atmosphere. When we do approach this problem again in the autumn, President de Gaulle will have visited the Soviet union and we shall have a clearer idea of the limits of military co-operation between France and the 14. Then, in reaching our decision, facts rather than expectations can guide us.
If two of the principal achievements of the meetings emerged out of conflict, the third important element-the emphasis on improving east-west relations-developed without opposition. Here, I am pleased to report, agreement was complete. All ministers recognized the need to increase bilateral contacts with the countries of eastern Europe. They saw this as having value in itself and as a necessity for the creation of an atmosphere propitious for the negotiations which must eventually take place on the German settlement. The ministers decided that a report on the possibilities for developing east-west relations should be prepared for their future use.
This unanimity of approach was most encouraging. It demonstrated the extent to which the members of the alliance share a common political outlook, agreeing on the aims of policy and on the prospects for making progress. All members reiterated that a European settlement was our basic objective. But the road to that settlement will be long. It is the intractability of the problems, rather than any lack of will to pursue solutions, which makes progress inevitably slow.
The proof of the measure of agreement and the motives underlying it are expressed in the final communique. By the standards of earlier communiques I regard this communique as forward looking. For this reason, and because it includes the formula agreed upon to cover negotiations with France and outlines certain changes in the structure of the organization, I have already asked the house, and we have agreed to its inclusion in Hansard.
The Brussels meeting can I think be described as fruitful in the sense that a week before the meeting began it seemed that we were headed for a confrontation between France and the 14 which threatened to lead to a complete breach. But a confrontation was avoided and a sense of shared interest prevailed. All countries agreed-and this is important-that the maintenance of the Atlantic alliance is as necessary today as ever. They further confirmed that, to this end, its members are pledged, separately and jointly, by means of continuous and effective
June 10, 1S66



self help and mutual aid, to maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack.
Our problems are not resolved, Mr. Speaker; indeed, the crucial issues have yet to be faced, but necessary preliminary decisions have been taken. For this we have the alliance and the NATO council machinery to thank. Once again, this time in new and in many ways more difficult circumstances, the value and the resilience of the alliance were demonstrated. We did our best to avoid unnecessary decisions which could have destroyed the alliance at this stage. We discussed many other problems, including Cyprus, but I have outlined today the essential ones because they involve the unity of the alliance. What the future holds for the 15 has yet to be determined but at any rate, as I have said, we have bought time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: NATO-REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Hon. members will, I know, join me in welcoming back to the house the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and will appreciate the fullness of the report he has given. This morning over the radio Ron Collister, who accompanied the minister, described him as a leader of the doves, a most unusual position for the minister to occupy.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
As far as the conference is concerned it was a most important one having, as it did, the responsibility of ensuring the preservation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and doing everything possible to keep France within that organization. France outside the organization would weaken NATO to an extent that would leave it little more than a memory.
It has been argued that NATO will benefit from the division that has taken place in consequence of the intransigent attitude of President de Gaulle. I think the answer to that was given by General M. Lemnitzer when he said "One more benefit of this sort and we will be out of business."
The minister quite frankly states that the problems are not resolved, that the issues that are crucial to the maintenance of NATO have been postponed. Sometimes there are victories in the postponement of action, and in this case I think we in the western world will agree that the fact that the confrontation which had been expected has been postponed at least permits us to hope that in the
23033-395J
External Affairs
intervening months between now and October the voices of reason will assure the preservation of NATO.
The minister also mentioned the necessity of improving east-west relations. Personally I feel that the Danish proposal for an early east-west conference was a worthy one. Careful preparations will have to be made before such a meeting can take place. Furthermore, there will have to be agreement among all the nations of NATO as to the basis upon which discussions may take place. I hope such a meeting can be arranged. It will be difficult. The experience since 1945 does not lead to an optimistic expectation as to the result. However, I think we must continue to pursue every avenue toward better relations with the U.S.S.R., particularly at this time when the U.S.S.R. and communist China are having their divisions and difficulties.
We are glad to have the assurance from the minister that deferring the question of moving the council was a major decision which was taken at the meeting. Had the 14 members of NATO proceeded with the removal of the council in the fact of the attitude taken by France, in my opinion to all intents and purposes NATO would have become a matter of history. All of us can hope that after General de Gaulle's visit to Moscow he will return with new concepts regarding NATO and its preservation.
It is of interest that President Tito has stated that the days of NATO are numbered and that this conference has established that result beyond any question of doubt. I do not accept his views, and I think Canadians as a whole will not accept them. He holds out the promise that if NATO goes, the Warsaw pact countries will dissolve their organization. We believe, with those who have the responsibility of government today, that NATO must be maintained, and that if changes must be made then, based on experience which has been gained since its inception, this should be done in a spirit that will make possible those changes. NATO has not outlived its usefulness. NATO must be preserved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we too welcome the Secretary of State for External Affairs back from Brussels. We have followed his statement with keen interest. Notwithstanding the withdrawal of France from the integrated military structure, it is clearly necessary to any effective military disposition to have the co-operation of France; and if it appears that Canada has

June 10, 1966
External Affairs
played a significant role in preventing decisions which might make that co-operation impossible in the future then I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs deserves our commendation and our thanks for taking this action on behalf of Canada. I believe Canadians generally would be averse to any course of action which would make co-operation with France more difficult.
There is, however, one aspect of this statement about which I feel very much less optimistic and less happy; that is where the minister discusses the third important element, as he calls the emphasis on improving east-west relations. He says this developed without opposition and that agreement was complete, that all ministers recognized the need to increase bilateral contacts with the countries of eastern Europe.
I do not doubt the value of bilateral contacts, but I suggest the time has come when the western alliance must be sued as a means of integrating policies of the whole alliance and moving toward the improvement of relations with the countries of eastern Europe. It is not good enough to have reliance upon bilateral arrangements to this end. After all, bilateral arrangements are bound to lead to a host of different and conflicting policies. To my mind the most important function of the alliance in the future will not be so much its military posture but whether it can transform itself into an instrument of integration of policies which eventually may lead to the dissolution of the alliance which after all is only a temporary measure to deal with a temporary situation. I am not happy if we are about to pat ourselves on the back about an agreement, if this only means that this course is to be pursued in a bilateral manner.
I noticed a guarded optimism on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he said the communique was good by past standards, or something of that sort. This indeed was very faint praise. He speaks with a degree of optimism chiefly because disaster has been averted. This is indeed better than nothing, but I want to urge upon the minister that he continue with efforts to make sure the alliance is ready to adopt not only a forward looking stance by previous standards, but a much more forward looking stance than has been the case in the past.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
I should like to say that any attempt to revive the past-and there seem to be some voices within the alliance that think this is possible-will mean the destruction and end of
(Mr. Brewin.]
the alliance. It is, therefore, with the hope that there will be a genuine transformation so that instead of this being forward looking from past, negative standards, there will be a truly forward look in the future that we commend the minister for what he has so far achieved, and in that sense we hope he is going to continue to take a bold, independent and forward approach to this whole problem on behalf of Canada.

subtopic: NATO-REPORT ON MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are also happy to observe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) is back in the house. All will admit, I think, that we missed his vast experience and his humour which are beneficial to the whole house.
It is obvious, having heard the statement of the minister, that all the problems discussed, considered and analysed by the NATO Council have not been settled by the meeting. Nothing was broken but nothing was settled. Discussions and decisions on the problems involved have been postponed, and further discussion has been made possible. That is all for the better, because if hurried decisions had been taken, they might possibly have been unfortunate.
The minister has played a major role in this meeting and I feel we ought to congratulate him for having prevented an unfortunate ending of the meeting.
Mr. Speaker, there is nevertheless, one fact that stands out in the report of the minister:	It is that the western powers
seemed to be lacking the presence of a strong man, of an experienced man capable of handling discussions with the eastern powers, and that man has turned out to be General de Gaulle, since the eyes of the western powers are now on his visit to Moscow, and everybody expects a lot to come out of it. If all the western powers expect a lot from such a visit, it is because they are confident that General de Gaulle is liable to return with concrete, positive and precise results.
The attitude of General de Gaulle may be questionable as far as NATO and the refusal of France to share in the integration of the armed forces is concerned.
Yet, we must not forget that NATO wanted to integrate everything, except the most important element of all. They wanted to integrate the military forces of 15 countries, but
June 10, 1966

only one country, the United States, would have kept control of the most important element today from the military point of view, in other words control of nuclear and atomic weapons. The other 14 countries would have given everything they had; the United States, on the other hand, would have given everything, except the most important thing of all, their atomic and nuclear weapons, which would not have been included in the integrated forces. It is not surprising that some countries did not like this attitude, particularly France, which protested.
All this leads us to believe that NATO has a new role to play. The active theatre of operations in external affairs is no longer Europe; it has shifted to another part of the world, to Asia. NATO was created in order to face any potential attack by countries of eastern Europe; on the other hand, the Warsaw Pact was intended to counterbalance NATO. The members of NATO and the Warsaw Pact must now realize that their role cannot be the same in the future. Pacts must no longer be concluded nor councils established in order to prepare for defence or war; instead, there should be councils or associations of countries working to spread peace in the world.
NATO's role must no longer be military but peaceful, because the active theatre of operations in external affairs has shifted from Europe to Asia. Therefore, I believe the role of NATO should be reviewed and reanalysed, and this is why I am glad to find that no definite decision was taken during the meeting in which the hon. minister took part.
Europe went through its own time of war; the people of Europe learned that war never brought anything pleasing, only destruction and death. Today, it seems that another part of the world has yet to find that out, and that is Asia. Well, Europe as well as America will have to see to it that decisions are taken to help those countries in Asia or Africa where fighting is going on to bring them back to peace, so that Canada will play in the world the role of pacification for which it has always been appreciated throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I join with the other party leaders in welcoming the Secretary of State for External Affairs back to the house. We have followed his activities with much interest, and I am sure all of us would say with a
Shipping
considerable degree of pride that we are pleased with the stand he has taken. Certainly I agree with what he said when he defined the major gain of this conference as that of gaining time; and if the stand he took, which was not always a popular one, was taken so that more consideration could be given to the difficult situation in which NATO finds itself due to unilateral decisions by France, I think something has been achieved. In view of the firm attitude taken by the United States and the situation which existed, I think perhaps we can best define the action taken as defensive action. We must commend the minister for his initiative in the broad, vital and important role he played. Of all the points he mentioned as being important, I think his reference to the need for agreement on and settlement of the European situation as being a common objective is the most important. The peace and stability of Europe, as related to the over-all situation brought into focus specifically by the action of France, can only be achieved on the basis of a settlement to bring the divided Germany together.
As others have already stated, what is now necessary at this stage is offensive action directed toward a redefinition of NATO and the new role it will play if it is to accomplish its objectives during this second phase of development in Europe, now that the danger of military action has eased off. I trust the minister will support this action in which he has already provided leadership, and use effectively Canada's re-established and strengthened position to define the new role for NATO, which certainly cannot be military but must be one dealing with economic and political aspects.
Let me again say that we are pleased that the minister is home. We appreciate the part he has been able to play for Canada, and in respect of his own personal leadership may we just say that his ability as an old pro politician has really shone forth in a commendable way.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SHORTAGE OF SILVER COINS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SHORTAGE OF SILVER COINS
speechtext: My question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Will the minister inform the house whether the government is now faced with an immediate and urgent problem relating to a shortage of coinage? If so, what action is proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SHORTAGE OF SILVER COINS
speechtext:
I do not believe a shortage of silver is likely to develop for some time to come. The decision of the United States to abandon the minting of silver coins in favour of coins made of copper and nickel has had the effect of greatly reducing the demand for silver. The treasury has indicated there is no immediate likelihood of a critical situation developing in connection with silver. It has stated its stocks of silver are sufficient for at least seven years ahead. The Canadian government has been aware for some time that Canada, like the United States, should make preparation in anticipation of any possible increase in the price of silver in the future.
For the last year the government has therefore been studying the possibility of substituting other metals for silver in our coinage.

Today, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) moves a similar amendment and every time an amendment of this nature is introduced, there are always members such as the previous speaker to say: Why place such things on our statutes?
Well, it is always time to do something intelligent. We have not had these things in our statutes in the past. At the present time, we hardly have 12 per cent French Canadians sitting on commissions. It is time for us to make a change.
What does it disturb if we have something definite on our statutes? All I ask is that we do not forget it and that, when they are preparing legislation, our ministers will not forget in the future to write it down, so that we do not have to do it through an amendment.

Some people talk about the immigrants coming into Canada; they say we ought to respect their language and their culture. I know that those who come to Canada, whether Poles, Italians, Germans, wherever they come from, whatever they are, know that by coming to Canada, they will have to learn at

However, when they come here, they cannot ask that the Treaty of Paris of 1763 be amended and that everything done since then be abolished. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister) moved

speechtext:
the second reading of the Bill No. C-174, to provide for the establishment of The Company of Young Canadians.
June 10. 1966

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity of moving the second reading of Bill No. C-174, an act to provide for the establishment of The Company of Young Canadians. This bill and the exciting adventure which the bill, if it is acceptable to parliament, will make possible is of great interest I am sure to all members of the house, as it is to me, as one step forward in the battle against poverty, disease, deprivation and inequality wherever these may exist in our country, as well as being a modest measure of assistance in meeting these problems in other countries.
The Company of Young Canadians represents the kind of constructive adventure in which I think we would all be glad to see our younger people, and perhaps some not so young, involved. In this respect the Secretary General of the United Nations, U Thant, expressed the other day the hope which I am sure many of us share. He said:
I am looking forward to the time when the average young person-and parent or employer- will consider that one or two years of work for the cause of development either in a far away country or in a depressed area of his own community is a normal part of one's education.
The Company of Young Canadians will, I believe, continue a good Canadian tradition reaching back to the Jesuit missions of New France right on down to the Grenfell medical outposts of Labrador and the bush-camp classrooms of frontier colleges. Its members will also serve in due course, if this legislation is approved, in villages and towns over the seas, in far away developing countries where already volunteers from the Canadian University Service Overseas-CUSO-are working and working with dedication and effectiveness. I hope that this company will be inspired by the same sense of high adventure and unselfish service as are the CUSO volunteers. For it is my hope, a hope which I am sure the house shares, that The Company of Young Canadians will have a useful, exciting and innovating role to perform in our national and in our international life.
The first reference to a Company of Young Canadians, as hon. members may recall, was made in the Speech from the Throne on April 5, 1965, a little more than a year ago, when there was this sentence in the speech:
You will be asked to approve the establishment of a Company of Young Canadians, through which the talents and energies of youth can be enlisted in projects for social development, both in Canada and abroad.
Company of Young Canadians
To ensure that plans for the company would reflect both the aspirations of young Canadians and the very real needs which the company might seek to meet in Canada and the developing countries, an organizing committee was appointed about a year ago to look into the idea and to formulate recommendations for the consideration of the government on which the government might be able to base legislation for submission to parliament.
Heading this organizing committee was a distinguished Canadian, Dr. Francis Leddy, now president of the University of Windsor, who had played an important role with Canadian University Service Overseas and World University Service of Canada, a man well equipped to be chairman of a committee to advise the government on a matter of this kind. We are grateful to him and to the members of his committee for the useful and unselfish service which they gave in the work which was transmitted to them.
The committee sought opinions from representatives of federal government departments, provincial governments, universities, voluntary agencies, youth groups and a number of private citizens. As a result of these consultations and discussions a report of the committee was submitted to the government last November.
Following a review of the recommendations of the committee and pending parliamentary consideration and action, the government announced its decision to proceed with a pilot program of voluntary service to Canada. At that time Mr. William McWhinney, who had been executive secretary of CUSO, was appointed interim director of the company. Since then the interim staff of the company has been reviewing project suggestions which have been received from government departments, federal and provincial, from organizations, from groups and from individuals all over Canada. The staff has also examined applications from many Canadians of all ages who have indicated their desire to take part in the company's operations when those operations begin.
Last month, Mr. Speaker, the government appointed an interim advisory council for the company to give advice to the government concerning proposed first year operations and to assist the staff of the company in carrying out certain pilot projects. The chairman of this advisory council is Mr. Douglas Ward, president-elect of the Canadian Union of Students, and the vice chairman Mr. Marc
June 10, 1966

Company of Young Canadians Lalonde, a distinguished lawyer from Montreal.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
When the organization committee made its report last November, it strongly recommended the need for the company to have a maximum degree of independence and flexibility, and the bill which is before the house for second reading embodies, I believe, that principle. It provides for the kind of freedom and manoeuvrability which will permit company volunteers in Canada and abroad to work in co-operation with a wide variety of groups and other agencies, both governmental and private. We hope also, Mr. Speaker, that the company will be encouraged to be experimental as well as responsible in its approach to problems, and that the company staff, council and volunteers will not be afraid to move into new and creative areas of social action.
The bill before the house provides for a council of 15 members, 10 of whom shall be elected by the volunteers themselves, with the other five appointed by the governor in council. This provision, Mr. Speaker, should ensure that the experience which volunteers gain in the field will be brought into the administrative affairs and management of the company. It indicates clearly that this is not only to be a company for young Canadians but a company of young Canadians, a company in which young Canadians themselves will play a major role in determining plans, operations and obectives.
The objects of the company, as hon. members perhaps know, are outlined in clause 14 of the bill, part of which reads:
-to support, encourage and develop programs for social, economic and community development in Canada or abroad through voluntary service.
Clause 15 of the bill outlines some of the areas in which the company may operate.
Before mentioning some of the specific projects which have been suggested for inclusion in this year's pilot program-incidentally, 60 such projects have been submitted to the interim organization of the company and 35 of these have been accepted as suitable for company action if parliament approves this legislation-and what they are concerned with, there are one or two general points which should be made about the programs in which company volunteers will participate.
Suggestions for company projects in Canada should, I believe, normally come from the people in the communities concerned. Suggestions should come from below and not


necessarily, or perhaps even normally, from above. The company should respond to express requests to have volunteers working in a particular community on a particular project, but volunteers would not be sent where they would not be needed or welcome. The Company of Young Canadians will not be able to fulfil its potential by sitting in offices in Ottawa and deciding what the volunteers will do and where they will do it.
Canadians through their organizations, through government departments and informal groups should be asked to make suggestions, as they have already done, about how the company volunteers could most effectively operate. Suggested projects in Canada which the company might support in its pilot program and in the years ahead have already, as I have said, been brought to the company's attention from communities, groups, individuals and agencies throughout the country by letter, by discussion groups and as a result of conferences.
We have felt, Mr. Speaker, that this approach is fundamental to the whole future of the company and will be essential, I think, if it is to realize its potential value. It will be quite wrong, as I see it, for the government or for the company itself to try to impose any program or any project on any group or community.
The nature of the proposed projects, and they are outlined in a general way in clause 15 of the bill, indicates the kind of work that it is expected the company will do. Some organizations have urged the government to provide volunteers for work in urban depressed areas where the volunteers would assist the residents of that particular area in identifying and understanding common problems and in considering ways and means of taking appropriate action to deal with them. These problems might relate to poor housing, inadequate recreational facilities, lack of language classes for new Canadians or poor counselling and home economics opportunities.
A number of Indian band councils have expressed an interest in having company volunteers assist them in various ways, in starting recreational programs, in assisting in the preparation of briefs and other documents for official agencies and governments, in developing local co-operatives and handicraft industries. Representatives of certain provincial governments have told the company of the need to work in their areas with high school drop-outs, assisting them in
June 10, 1966	COMMONS
finding jobs or in preparing for job opportunities. Indian and Metis organizations have requested volunteers to help in developing social and recreational activities for their members and in helping to make sure of school educational opportunities.
The company staff has been told of the many difficulties encountered by many immigrants who come to Canada and need assistance in learning French or English and in adapting to the different characteristics of their new country. It is felt that the company could help here.
Some provincial government representatives have emphasized the need for community development programs, especially in rural areas where the company could, it was felt, be helpful. There were as well representations from some rural groups for assistance in starting community health or educational programs.
It is important to note, Mr. Speaker, that in all such proposed projects or programs the company would operate only in co-operation with the many other organizations and agencies already in the field which are already attempting to deal with these social and economic problems.
Company volunteers will not necessarily be experts nor will they have a ready mix of preconceived notions to apply to whatever community situation they may discover. Their approach will be to help the people of the community decide what should be done and to work with them in the doing of it.
During the first year of the company's operations volunteers will work only within Canada. This will be during the first year. Already excellent work has been carried out by Canadian University Service Overseas volunteers since 1961. It was decided to concentrate during this initial period on domestic programs while considering how the company's future international role could be most effectively undertaken.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I think all Canadians can be justifiably proud of the 550 Canadian men and women who have gone to the developing countries under CUSO sponsorship. The government itself has shown its confidence in CUSO through the increased financial help which has been granted by parliament. It is my hope that the formation of The Company of Young Canadians will make it possible in the future for many more Canadians to participate in overseas service. To that end, the staff and advisory council of the company are now

Company of Young Canadians studying ways in which the company can undertake international assignments, and discussions are now being held with CUSO representatives to consider areas of co-operation, to avoid overlapping or duplication.
In domestic projects, company volunteers will fill only those positions which will not otherwise be filled from the existing labour force; they will do work which would not ordinarily be done by the labour force. In other words, volunteers will not be used as cheap labour.
It is expected that in the first year of operations a wide variety of projects concerning many different segments of the population will be undertaken so that future programs can be based on the most thorough field experience possible.
From time to time, since the announcement concerning the company was first made, I have been asked whether the government feels that young Canadians are ready to discharge the heavy and important responsibilities which will be theirs in the organization. This is an easy question to answer. In the last few years we have witnessed an immensely exciting and stimulating resurgence of social concern and responsibility on the part of young people The way in which young Canadians have responded to CUSO's appeal for volunteers willing to spend two years working abroad in developing countries is evidence of this new spirit. There are other organizations, expecially some of the student and religious organizations, which draw on this desire for participation which is so strong among Canada's young people.
Though there may be some exciting exceptions which prove this rule, the younger generation today possesses idealism without illusion; realism without cynicism. These young people desire to make a forceful and direct contribution to the kind of society they feel is worth living in, working for and fighting for, and I hope this feeling will find concrete expression in The Company of Young Canadians.
The applications already received by the company show that our confidence in young Canadians has not been misplaced. More than 2,500 of these inquiries and applications have already been received, even before the legislation has been passed, and they show a great diversity of background and interest. Many of those who have applied are undergraduates or recent graduates of universities-30 per cent to date. Others are attending or have graduated from high schools-45 per cent to

Company of Young Canadians date. Others have been out working, often for as long as 20 or 30 years and wish now to take on this kind of voluntary service for two years. Forty per cent of all applications received have been from young women. The minimum age for volunteers is 18 but there is no upper age limit-this will enable them to accommodate the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh).

Although the vast majority, about 85 per cent, are in the age group 18 to 25, a number of applications have been received, as I have already noted, from people in their forties, fifties and sixties and it is to be hoped that many people in this age bracket, young in spirit, will find an opportunity to express their social concern through working with the company.
Volunteers will be selected on the basis of their personal qualities, their experience in working with other people and their ability to work effectively in a particular company project. They will take part in a six weeks orientation program before proceeding to their assignments. This program will emphasize aptitudes in human relations, community development techniques, and knowledge of the region and community where the volunteer will work. Once the volunteers are in the field, they will be called together from time to time to evaluate their experience and to take part in further learning sessions. When in the field, they will have the support and advice of people from the agency which is sponsoring their project, other local persons and members of the company staff. They will be granted allowances for food and accommodation, and for expenses appropriate to their projects. They will also receive a small personal allowance. Upon completion of their term of service, they will receive a small honorarium for each month of service.
Any assessment of the impact and importance of The Company of Young Canadians must, of course, await the experience of the first year's program. But we can be reasonably sure about some things. While the volunteer is making a contribution to the social, economic or cultural development of a community, he will also be learning from the people with whom he works. A two-way learning process will be an integral part of every project. If the evidence of similar organizations is any indication, volunteers who serve in the company will leave it as

better citizens, committed to a renewed concern for their fellowmen and a clearer understanding of the processes of change which are so essential to any dynamic and democratic society.
I hope the company, through its volunteers, will have a stimulating, creative effect upon our society and its institutions, and will also help the people of new nations overseas. I believe the company will prove to be an organization deeply concerned with the fundamentals of inequality and poverty in our society and with social justice and democratic progress, and that it will become part of our continuing search for a better Canada in a better world. It is in this spirit that I ask for the support of the house on the second reading of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is part, I believe, of a world wide recognition of a fundamental fact, namely that the society of the nations of the world cannot continue with the rich becoming richer and the poor relatively poorer.
When one looks at the situation domestically and recognizes the tremendous gap between those who have their foot on the ladder and are sharing in the growing wealth of a modern industrial nation like Canada, and the fact that there is a substantial group in our country, I would say approximately 20 per cent, who do not seem to have the ability or the opportunity to get on that first step of the ladder, then one realizes the size of the task before us.
But if one projects his mind to the situation all over the world where a great majority know that in spite of all their efforts over the next 35 years the best they can do is raise their per capita income from $100 a year to $170 a year, a gain of 70 per cent, while at the same time industrial nations expect to double their per capita income, again using round figures, from $2,500 to $5,000, one can see that the gap between $100 and $2,500, as it is now, will be much greater 35 years from now when the gap is between $170 and $5,000. I am using very broad figures covering the whole industrial segment of the world as opposed to the newly developing segments.
These two sets of facts are the challenge before the countries of the world today. This bill is an attempt by the government to bring Canada into this movement to try and bridge this gulf not only at home but abroad. As
June 10, 1966

such I do not think there is a Canadian in the country who does not give his approval to the aims and purposes of this legislation.
I cannot go so far as to say that I think this is going to work easily, because I know it is not, but I do think it is something upon which the government should be congratulated. I shall admit immediately that the government copied the American precedent. One month after President Johnson, in his address on the state of the nation, coined the phrase, "A war on poverty" we had a "Company of Young Canadians" suggested to us. It is copied obviously after the Peace Corps and after the program called Vista-Volunteers in Service to America.
But even though it is copied after the Americans, that is not fatal to the idea. What concerns me more is the point that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) dealt with in his speech, namely the tremendous desire of young people in every country of the world to serve. A generation ago people were idealistic, but sentimentally idealistic. They were the type of people who would serve their country behind great slogans like "A war to save democracy," and "A war to end discrimination."
We pay honour to those generations; but today the fact is that we have a new type of generation on our hands, a generation which is not sentimental and which does not believe these sentimental bromides that so many of us followed, and that some of us still follow. The young generation today has idealism, a cynical type of idealism, but it takes the form of wanting to participate. They want to be part of the action.
This leads me to the main concern I have about the legislation now before us. The concern that I have is that, with all this tremendous willingness of 10 per cent, 20 per cent or 30 per cent of our young people leaving high schools and leaving universities who want to be part of the action to help at home and abroad, and their willingness to volunteer in their hundreds and thousands, if this program does not give them full opportunity and full challenge, if it leaves thejn dissatisfied, feeling that there is lack of organization, that they are not doing an effective job, or if this program sends them into operations unprepared, the disillusionment that comes so quickly to young people will be disastrous for the concepts that this legislation entails.
Company of Young Canadians
This is the fear that some of us have, some of us who have been thinking along the idea of doing something in an active way to meet this challenge of today. Looking at this legislation, and looking at what has been done in the United States and here to date, this is one fear that does engulf us. If these young people lose their idealism, if they are not fully used in this program, if the challenges are not every day greater than their abilities so that they know they are doing something useful, and if they are not succeeding-because there never will be success in this type of program if these factors are lacking-and if as a result they feel disillusionment, the result with this type of program in the future will, as I said, be disastrous.
I have expressed this concern in a general way. I have known young men of my own generation and young men and women of this generation, and I can assure the house that the young men of this generation will not be as patient as we were in ours. We were impatient in our own way; we rebelled in many ways, but we would accept. The young generation will not be as patient as we were in our time, and the generation ahead of us were in their time. If they do not get satisfaction immediately that they are doing a good job and a well organized job, then the very nature of their being today, which is to be activist, will lead to a disillusionment that will spread and cause serious harm to this concept.
Talk to the young men who have served in our armed forces for this last 10 years. They go in full of idealism; they want to serve their country. They are willing to spend part of their time at university in military service. They are willing to accept lower wages during summer in order to be in the armed forces and serve their country. But after two or three years you usually find the vast majority of these young men with their morale down, with disillusionment in the military and disillusionment in the government, because in the final analysis it always comes back to that place.
This does not make me glad. It bothers me, because their disillusionment spreads to others who are not quite as idealistic, and if this attitude develops in this country it bodes ill for the future. I think I have said enough on this point to indicate what I think is the chief danger ahead. I believe it can be overcome. I believe it can be met if the government is willing to move slowly and deliberately through its officials to lay down what the

Company of Young Canadians problem is, lay down the procedures, and train these young people properly.

If I may, I would like at this time to suggest the way that some of us would have liked to do this. The problem we are talking about is not new. Those of us who approach these things carefully, and in the long run we believe that to be the most successful way, always like to know where we are going. In the party to which I belong this problem was one of our major concerns. On the agricultural front we introduced the legislation known as ARDA. The house may recall that in the debate which made that bill into a statute I opposed my own legislation on third reading. Because there was no opposition on second reading-everyone seemed to be in favour of the idea of ARDA-I felt it was my duty to point out to the house that there were dangers. The dangers which I pointed out are not too unlike what I point out today. I am glad I opposed my own legislation on ARDA, because it made clear to those administering the program what I felt were the danger points. I think they have benefited by that warning and have tended to move slowly and carefully into this very difficult area.
The dangers are very simple and yet very complex. The two main difficulties in dealing with any kind of a program concerning poverty or the lack of use of human resources are, first of all, educational, and secondly sociological. If you examine the work to date in the three main aspects of the war on poverty in the United States, you will find in nearly every case that these two factors are the things which come to the surface and which are causing trouble. Of course in the United States the trouble was that somebody had a brilliantly idealistic idea and, being typically American, they rushed into it, set up a program, called for volunteers and rushed into battle. Now they are trying to assess their difficulties and fight their way out of the messes which need not have occurred had they taken proper precautions.
As the house may remember, in 1962 the prime minister of that day, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) proposed a national conference on human resources. This proposal was made because after our study of the problem we recognized that within the confines of the civil service, for the advice of ministers, there was insufficient information and there were insufficient ideas to successfully tackle this problem. We recognize that it would take two or three

DEBATES	June 10, 1966
years of searching through the whole world for people in the social science field who had ideas as to how to tackle this problem, and whom we could bring to our conference where, with the preliminary preparation which had been made in advance, we could have a long slow deliberate discussion so that we would be in a position to lay down the guide lines not only for the senior governments at the provincial and federal level but also for the local governments, the individuals across the country and particularly the hundreds of little organizations which now deal with this type of problem.
When one counts up the number of organizations in a large metropolitan city which deal domestically with this type of problem, the figure runs into the hundreds, not the scores. Therefore overlapping and confusion is the greatest single difficulty in the big urban centres. Our concern was to bring together the best minds of the world in an effort to see, when sitting down with the representatives of government, these organizations and individuals, whether we could agree on the precise nature of the problems and the course of action to take in respect of each particular type of problem.
Let me mention some of these problems. One of the great tragedies of modern day living is the fact that in our built-up communities we have hundreds of thousands of people whom we classify as aged. An aged person may be a person who has been pensioned off at age 55. There are many of those; an example would be the members of our armed services. There are many whose jobs have changed, who are pensioned off and who cannot find new employment. In general language they are classified as being aged.
Second, through technological changes in the field of health, man no longer is an old person at age 60, 65, 70 or 75; it depends on the individual. So we have many thousands of people in the very prime of their mental ability who are cut off because of pension policies and because of rules in industry and in the professions. Here you have a tremendous unused human resource which has tremendous potential and which could fill a need in this area. This potential is not being utilized because it is not being organized. In this group of aged I include the housewife whose family is raised. The woman who is, say 45 or 50 years of age, still has some of her skills from the days when she was working and now is much more experienced in looking after individuals. Yet in many cases
June 10, 1966	COMMONS
this very effective person is left to amuse herself with curling games, bridge games, sometimes gardening, and so on. This is an unused human resource which can become a burden on society because of frustrations, and in extreme cases mental health problems. We can utilize that human resource for greater productivity and for the greater enjoyment of the people of the country.
The problems of the aged people are not all problems of health. There is the problem of utilization. This is one field in which there is a tremendous amount of information available in respect of the type of programs which could be worked out in communities of every size for people of every skill and background. This material should be collected and put into the hands of an organization such as the one being created by this bill, so that the organization would have something to work with.
When you go into the field of the handicapped, it is only 20 years ago that people who were deaf and who were blind were considered to be seriously handicapped. Now the social scientist knows that in many forms of activity the person who is deaf has an advantage over the hearing person, and the person who cannot see has tremendous advantages over the seeing person. Let us go down the list of the handicapped. We come to the spastic. Until the last ten years in many, and perhaps most, of the countries in the western world the only social disposition we could make of them was to bring them out of the home in which they were hidden and put them in an institution. Now we have many places where the spastic can be rehabilitated and where with physiotherapy treatment and teaching, depending on his mental ability, he is able to go into almost any occupation, although there probably would be an exception in the case of surgery and jewelry work.
The work done in respect of spastics in this past ten years is a revelation. This is a unique human resource. However, in Canada as yet there is no definite program for spastics. There are, let us say 20,000, available persons in this country at any age. We are not using the knowledge which is available. We are not using and organizing the type of information we have. When we get to the retarded, we find we have made tremendous progress in this field in the last 15 years. In Canada we have gone as far as putting up sheltered workshops for them. This type of sheltered workshop is so obsolete in the new knowledge that no modern social scientist wants to speak of it any longer. Yet in Canada we have not made any attempt to

The answers are very simple, once you know them. Everyone knows if you can break down a complicated industrial task into simple components so that even a five-year-old can do them, then it does not matter whether that five-year old mind is in a forty-year-old body or not, that individual can match the efficiency of any workman doing the job in the country. This same principle applies to the delinquents of this country. The desire of young people to take action and to belong to groups that are different from their seniors is motivated by a force that can be used for good purposes. I am not suggesting that the only answer is to teach them to wear tight pants, pointed shoes, long hair and to beat guitars, although that is how the energy of certain young people of Liverpool was used. I have dealt with the two sections of the human resources of our country in respect of which some effort must be made, the aged and the handicapped. I could go on and list many other groups, but what I am trying to say is that, just as under ARDA, where we tried to develop a concept which would meet the needs of those many thousands of people living on the land who were not able to take advantage of the opportunities around them, in order to give them a chance to earn a better income, so here could we develop a concept which would give similar opportunities to the people living in cities.
I am always concerned when I read what is happening in relation to the horrible "snafus" that are taking place in various areas of the United States, resulting in a tremendous amount of idealism and enthusiasm being turned into an unholy mess. Company of Young Canadians
I am not pessimistic about the future, but with all the strength at my command I am trying to give warning of the danger that exists because the task we are undertaking and must accomplish in dealing with those who need help is extemely important. After reading this bill and listening to the Prime Minister today my fears are confirmed. I was waiting to hear the problems outlined and specific guide lines laid down. There is nothing in this bill that gives a clear-cut concept of what is to be done. The Prime Minister was vague in his remarks, and one can understand why I am concerned.
I approach this whole problem naturally as a Conservative would. In 1962 it was suggested that we should have a national conference on human resources. I still believe that such a conference must be held in order to collect together this tremendous amount of knowledge from social scientists around the world so that guide lines can be adopted to provide some tangible program for the group of people administering this legislation to follow.
When I think of the individual who will head this operation I am sorry for him. He will be faced with problems similar to those faced by the communists in Russia in 1917 to 1928 when all they had to follow was the doctrine of Karl Marx. It took those people 20 years to decide that they should push his doctrine aside and find something which would make their system work in practice. Karl Marx did not deal with practical problems of human civilization; he dealt with ideas. It is one of our modern miracles that the Russians were able to survive as a nation. In order to realize this one need only read his work, Das Kapital. The same thing applies to the Chinese. Imagine their trying to build a socialized nation on the teachings of Karl Marx and the precedents of experience in Russia. Thank heaven the Chinese are very pragmatic people and can learn from the mistakes of others.
In any event, the situation will be similar for the individual who heads this organization, using this bill and the Prime Minister's speech as a guide. The only thing I can suggest is that by prayer we had better turn this whole matter over to the power above, because certainly there is no guidance coming from the government.
The reasons I have not dealt with sociology in detail in Canada are I think self-evident. If the Prime Minister searched through all the civil service agencies here in Ottawa and across the country and found five practising

sociologists he would be lucky. When I was minister I could only find one practising, and another working on a farm outside Ottawa because he could not find employment in his field of learning. Yet the lack of men experienced in this field will in effect be the rock upon which ARDA will founder and the rock upon which this program will founder.
Sociology is a big word, but in plain terms it means knowing how people think. If you want a farmer to do something which you know is good, would you send a young kid fresh out of school wearing a white shirt to discuss the situation with that farmer; and if you did, do you think he would be successful? I suggest that such action could only be classified as conspiracy to murder. If you want an individual who has lived in the slum areas of our cities for years to act differently and do things differently, do you send an idealistic individual to teach him how to live in a home under our modern concepts? Speaking in the crude language which has been ascribed to me by the Prime Minister, let me suggest that we must learn to back into a beer parlour. You must appear to be looking one way while going another: That is sociology. You must bring a person to the point of wanting to do what you think is good for him.

I want this legislation to succeed, but I have in all intellectual honesty to point to what I think are the dangers. I think we will still need some form of national conference of human resources. That may take two or three years to get ready. The educational program will stem from this. You will then give the organization something tangible with which to work. There will be a tremendous amount of time spent in obtaining the properly trained person, because you have to deal with not only the farmer and people who are poor but the juvenile delinquent brought up in a slum district, and so on. There are many people around who are properly qualified. You do not get them by snapping your fingers. It will take time. If I have been facetious, Mr. Speaker, it is because I feel deeply about these matters and want to get my point across to the house.
The second point with which I wish to deal concerns the age factor. The recruits will be mostly from the age group 18 to 30. I am not quarrelling with that. There is also the suggestion that the age can go up to 50. This is the point I want to speak about. I think there are two stages in a person's life when the urge to do something for his fellow man is paramount. The first stage is coming out of high school and university when a certain percentage of our young people, freed with the little bit of knowledge they have obtained, want to go forward and help others. What the percentage is, we do not know; but I think it is substantial-10, 20 or 30 per cent. That person eventually becomes married, has a house to buy and a car, all the other things to acquire, children to educate, and so on. For a period of 25 years he is usually lost to this form of idealistic enterprise of helping others. Therefore the time to get people to serve in this type of operation is in the age group from high school to university. I think this is covered in the bill.
The second group are those people from 45 up, who in our modern economy have usually reached high enough in their professions and job classification that they feel they have come to the end of their upward progress. If

Company of Young Canadians one examines the civil service at the provincial or federal level, he finds that in the pyramids of people forcing their way up are few places at the top. Many, many people at the middle levels are tremendously capable but there are only one or two spots at the top. These people at the middle levels have raised their families; they have great ability and experiance. If a recruiting program in this age group were carried out it would yield in the long run more effective workers than would be obtained at the younger level. This applies to medical people and those in all the professions.
At the age of 45 or 50 many of these people feel they have done well in their profession; their income is satisfactory and they would like to do something very, very useful for the 20 or 30 years they have left. I could quote the names of many Canadians who fit into this category and demonstrate my point. Using my own province as an example, there is Dr. Hardy, who was Dean of Engineering of the University of Saskatchewan. He spent 15 of the happiest years of his life serving in Ceylon. Every three years he came home to Canada on leave. As I say, Mr. Speaker, this was a great man at the University of Saskatchewan. But there comes a time when you are a little tired of teaching class after class of engineering students about farm machinery. He went to a country that needed him. Any man who ever spoke to Dr. Hardy recognized that here was a happy man, a man at the full height of his intellect, a man who wanted to use the years left to him on behalf of those who needed his help most.
Dr. Harrington, who is now with FAO, is one of the great plant biologists in the world. He left our province and served in Egypt, Israel, and is now with FAO. This is a happy man. He was at the top of his profession in Canada. He is now providing huge benefits to those he is serving. A doctor 50 years of age came to me a year ago and asked if he could serve abroad. I tried to get him into China, because that is where he wanted to go, but apparently we do not recognize China so he ended up in Africa. That man is a successful surgeon and is now providing tremendous benefits to those he is serving in Africa. I know that people of this age group would supply a tremendous number of recruits.
The practical proposal with regard to people in the civil service, the teaching profession, or those in private, professional occupations is to provide them, if they are civil

Company of Young Canadians servants, with a guarantee that when they come back to this country their pension will be intact. If this is done they will use their talents in a new country, knowing that when they return to Canada their pension will be there. We tried to do this, as a government. At the United Nations the prime minister of that day suggested that Canada would be glad to set up a bank of brains to help the underdeveloped nations of the world. This bank of brains was to come from the older people. I think we set this program up so that any person who wanted to go abroad would have his pension protected. I do not think the program was sufficiently advertised or sold to the people. Our government was a failure in public relations, even on good ideas.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am going to ask the house to join with the Prime Minister and pass this legislation. I shall join with the Prime Minister in this respect and hope that the legislation will start Canada on the task of developing opportunities for young people with ideas and ability to help themselves and also to help others. I know of the dangers ahead and I know of the pitfalls that will very likely lie in the path of this operation. I have described in my own way some of the pitfalls in dealing with human nature in our own country. I would suggest that these pitfalls are the same abroad. In addition, when these young people, and perhaps some of the older people, go abroad they should learn that in these newly developing nations they will have to contend with nationalism the like of which they have never known before. They will have to contend with discrimination the like of which they have never known before.
It is very good for the person whose skin is white to be in the minority in a country where the skin of the majority is a different colour and to realize that he is the odd person and the one who suffers discrimination. If they can learn to recognize that in these ancient lands they do have their own cultures-and some of the cultures of Asia are far superior in many ways to our own; and in Africa, even though they may have tribal cultures, they are their cultures-and can learn the humility of accepting the fact that this is the culture of these people and their civilization, and remember that all you do is stir up antagonism, dislike and, yes, hatred if you walk around with the typical air of superiority of the white man, they will be able to help these people very much more.


These things are sociological and have to be learned, and if there is a genuine desire, as I am sure there is, on behalf of Canadians and many other people to help others, if we can train our people to move into these fields as humble servants of a greater cause than just themselves, I believe that great good both at home and abroad can come from this kind of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Social Credit party and as far as my own personal support of this project is concerned I am pleased to identify our members with this legislation and to give it our approval here in this chamber, as the bill passes through its various stages into legislation. I think this Company of Young Canadians represents the type of project which we should have within our own national development; and I must say that I have had a very personal interest in it ever since it was first mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
I say this because during the early years of the war, which is now more than 20 years ago, it was my personal privilege to accept a similar challenge as that represented in the objectives of The Company of Young Canadians, and as a result was able to lead a team of Canadians to Ethiopia, which was the first country liberated in world war II. Not
June 10, 1966
knowing what we were heading into, but being aware of the tremendous needs created by the conflict in that African country, we found ourselves faced with the challenge of fitting into a picture which included every possible phase of need, as far as the people of what might be called a primitive society were concerned-needs of education, as well as in the areas of health and community development.
Most of us were able to spend a good part of our adult years in what I would consider to be the type of project with which The Company of Young Canadians will be concerned. I have always been very grateful for this opportunity, Mr. Speaker. As 1 have watched our own young people grow up, I have always been of the conviction that, if a similar opportunity could be provided to more of our young people, not only would they be able to render a very useful service to humanity but it would also be a tremendous experience for them.
The real benefit of a project such as this is twofold. It is of direct benefit as far as the service rendered is concerned; and there are surely any number of needs, some of them urgent and vital, waiting to be met not only at home but particularly in the developing countries of the world. Then there is also a very real benefit to be gained by those who take part in providing this type of service, a type of benefit that will not only help the individual but will also prove of tremendous value to the community in which he lives and in later years to the country itself.
As a result of my experience in Africa I was able to watch the developing years of the Peace Corps movement from the United States. I hope that the work of young Canadians in foreign lands, as it has developed through CUSO, Crossroads Africa and other private projects, will not follow exactly the same pattern as did the Peace Corps. Yet I have been tremendously impressed with the work the Peace Corps has done. I have been even more impressed with the result this experience has had on the lives of those who were part of it.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I think we could say this about the work of the CUSO organization. In a very quiet and typically Canadian way hundreds of our young people have gone out and have been doing work in foreign countries, a job similar to that intended to be done by The Company of Young Canadians at home.

Company of Young Canadians
A day or so ago I received an explanatory statement defining the purposes and projected types of activity of The Company of Young Canadians. For the sake of the record, though I realize the Prime Minister already has referred to this in introducing the legislation, it might be well to quote from this bulletin. We are told that the main purpose of The Company of Young Canadians will be-
-to provide assistance to individuals and communities to overcome some of the problems of poverty, injustice and inequality which exist in society. The company will do this by recruiting and assigning full-time volunteers to projects for social, economic and community development In Canada and abroad. It is being established not only in response to the very real needs for voluntary service, but also in response to the growing interest and concern of young Canadians to participate in constructive social action.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we see that the role of The Company of Young Canadians, as has already been stated, has not so much to do with economic development or the material development of our own nation, but rather, with human resources. Surely this is the area where we ought to show greater concern than we have. Surely we also ought to be concerned with advancing the potentialities that are latent in the young people we have in our country. I hope that this organization, in working toward the fulfilment of its objectives, will be primarily concerned with this.
One thing that I have been concerned about, with respect to The Company of Young Canadians, was the slowness evident in defining its purposes and in laying out the pattern of its organization. I trust after this length of time a solid foundation has been provided today for the organization which is to develop and take shape out of the legislation before us at the present time.
In The Company of Young Canadians we have a great tradition involving the historical pattern of the past in our young country. As we look back into our history and think of the great explorers, the great adventurers, and of the great developments in recent years in areas of industry and commerce, we realize that many of the deeds carried out were performed by young people.
In the growing collectivism that surrounds us, and in the pattern of greater public participation in many things which were regarded the responsibility and the opportunity of the individual not so long ago, we perhaps have been guilty of neglecting the type of individual who has played such a vital part in our historical past. Through The Company

6270	COMMONS
Company of Young Canadians of Young Canadians there will be provided an opportunity for the young people of today to repeat, and perform in their own right, actions which belong to the heritage of our past.
I note in the legislation, Mr. Speaker, that the area of activity of The Company of Young Canadians is to be both national and international. May I make a cautionary remark about the latter aspect of activity, before speaking briefly about the former. It has not been indicated to us what form the foreign operations of The Company of Young Canadians will take. I think it is necessary for the organization itself to define this as soon as possible. May I say that I hope The Company of Young Canadians will not be moving directly into the area of foreign operations undertaken by such organizations as CUSO. When one compares the activities of the CUSO organization with, shall we say, the Peace Corps of the United States, it becomes apparent that one of the great assets of the CUSO organization is that it is not labelled with the stigma of being a foreign government agency. Although the Peace Corps of the United States has performed a very commendable service, repeatedly in foreign countries where the people are swayed by various types of propaganda the Peace Corps volunteers have been labelled as working for a government agency.
CUSO volunteers overseas have lived and worked on the same level as the nationals among whom they are, and by entering into what are called "local contracts", rather than by being the employees of a foreign agency, have been able to fit into the communities and to reach their objectives in a commendable way. On the other hand, while those in the Peace Corps serve without remuneration, the people serving with it live at a standard higher than those they are serving who are of comparative education and qualification. This has not been done with CUSO, where the volunteers have accepted local conditions, giving them a clearer understanding of local problems, and bringing to them the confidence of the people they are serving.
While I think it would be unwise for The Company of Young Canadians to set up an organization which would either replace or supplement the CUSO volunteers, I would hope in the years ahead that the company might move in to support and co-operate with the CUSO organization. I realize that some of the young people who are involved in The
