Company of Young Canadians now, particularly Mr. McWhinney, have spoken about this in the past, so that it is perhaps not necessary to repeat what has been said.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I wish to emphasize the need to preserve such commendable efforts. There may be a temptation, in the desire to move ahead more rapidly, to take over CUSO. I think it would be tragic if any such move were made. To sum up, I believe the Company of Young Canadians ought not move into the area of foreign service but should support the organizations which are already active in this field, and rather help to make them more effective in fulfilling their responsibilities and achieving their objectives. Of all the spontaneous movements which have developed in the post-war years with the object of helping countries less fortunate than ourselves, CUSO heads the list. I am sure all of us who have had first-hand experience of the work being done in those countries will agree with this. It is my hope that the new organization will take full cognizance of this, and work to strengthen CUSO rather than replace it.
As to the company's activities on the home front, this is another story altogether. I notice that a report by the organizing committee called attention to three needs which the company should help to meet. First there are the needs of economically and socially deprived persons in Canada and overseas. I am speaking now about Canada. In this area one of the most urgent and challenging problems concerns our native Canadian people, the Eskimos and the Indians. A great many opportunities present themselves to an organization such as the one we are considering. In my own constituency, for example, there are three small Indian reserves all located not far from what might still be called the frontier town of Rocky Mountain House. How is one to integrate the activities, the education and the social life of young people growing up on these reserves? That is a real problem.
The people of this town, trying to meet their responsibilities, are now setting up a community centre for the use of these young Indian people. They are not sure just how it will operate. Everyone recognizes the need for such a centre and the people of the community sincerely desire to do something to help these young people.
I believe these volunteers could move in and do a tremendous job in connection with a project such as this. In fact I hope one of the first projects supported by the company at
June 10, 1966

home will be one such as this in my own constituency. I know that a similar need exists in many other areas. I do not think there is another field in Canada where our young people could perform a more effective service than they could in this type of project among our aboriginal people.
The organizing committee's report speaks, also, of the need of young people for more adequate channels through which young people could direct their ideals. I agree with this. In our changing society there is, indeed, a need to provide opportunities for constructive service for our young people-channels into which could be directed the energy, idealism and vision which is characteristic of them and which, all too often, they have no opportunity to express.
The third point made by the committee is also important-the need of our society as a whole for "domestic experimentation based on the constructive inter-action of the two groups". As I have indicated, I believe it would be better for the organization to concern itself directly with projects on the home front and co-operate with organizations already working overseas. In the years ahead, as more experience is gained, a better defined pattern of procedure will emerge and a more effective way found of reaching the goals which are the intent of the bill before us.
I do not know how the organization expects to finance its operations. It appears from this legislation that the public purse is expected to provide a major part of the funds required. I would add a cautionary word: It would be wrong for the organization to divorce itself completely from the support which might be obtained from the private sector of the economy. I am not thinking now of donations which might come from large organizations in industry and commerce or from the bigger social organizations across Canada. I am thinking of community participation.
I visualize these young people becoming in many ways direct community leaders as they go out to the tasks assigned to them. I believe there should be provision for community participation in the financial burdens which the programs will represent as well as in the programs themselves.
There is much more which could be said about the policy and objectives; more speculation as to how this program might develop. But I do not think this is really the time to enter upon a debate of this sort, since we are
Company of Young Canadians concerned, now, with fundamental principles-the basic objectives of the legislation before us.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We are pleased therefore to support the principle of this legislation, and we shall reserve further remarks until we go into the details of it. Again I want to emphasize that we need such a program. We support the intended purposes of it, and we trust that as it moves forward into reality it will successfully reach the objectives that have been defined during presentation of the legislation and by the organizing committee.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my enthusiasm for this bill. For the past few years I have been closely associated with young Canadians, both as a lecturer at college in Montreal, and this year by having the good fortune of being president of the Canadian Newman Club. I have also in past years worked closely with the World University Service of Canada and the International Student Centre in Montreal.
I want to assure the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the government that young Canadians welcome this legislation and the opportunities it will present. For many years they have been interested in international service. As far back as 1948 the World University Service of Canada initiated international seminars held in other countries to study the problems of those countries. This year such a seminar is being held in Turkey.
When the Peace Corps was established in the United States many university students and others in Canada looked forward to the day when we could have a similar organization here. As a matter of fact many Canadians attempted to become involved in the Peace Corps. Immediately following that time CUSO was started and, as has been mentioned, has already done a great deal of work in this field.
I am glad to see that clause 2(e) provides that all ages and classes of Canadians will be able to associate themselves with The Company of Young Canadians. In an earlier speech I pointed out that there are many older people, especially people who have retired from the professions, people who have made their mark in Canadian life, such as doctors, teachers, lawyers and engineers, who still have a lot of good work left in them and who have indicated they would like to go abroad and to other parts of Canada to help those who need help.
6272	COMMONS
Company of Young Canadians
I was also glad to hear the Prime Minister say that many non-university graduates have applied to work with the company. It would be a great mistake if it were to be dominated by university graduates. I hope in years to come the company will embrace young tradesmen, young farmers, 4-H workers, and just plain workers who can play a part in the program.
As a lawyer I am interested in seeing a project established similar to that of the neighbourhood law office in the United States. If we could get law students, young law graduates and other interested people to give legal assistance to people who cannot afford it, this would be a useful project.
It would also be a good idea, since many organizations of this type are being formed throughout the world, if we could work in conjunction with them, to the extent of forming an international youth corps. Once we get started we should approach the Peace Corps in the United States and similar corps throughout the world, to form international teams to work in other countries.
In other words, instead of having Canadian teams or American teams working abroad, we could have teams composed of volunteers from Canada, the United States, France, Germany and England. We could even invite Americans to come into Canada to work with young Canadians in the north, and send Canadians to work with the Peace Corps in the United States. This would promote an international rather than a national spirit.
It has been said that The Company of Young Canadians may provide young Canadians of the sixties with the same sort of opportunities to serve in an idealistic way that armies did in past years and centuries. However, I would hate to view Canadians serving abroad in a nationalistic or paternalistic way, and that is why I hope some day to see this work being done on an international basis.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to add my voice in enthusiastic support of this measure, and I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the government for bringing it forth.
Unlike the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) I will not apologize for my old age, because I have not attained that. I hope to live so long that some day I will be as old as I look, but right now I am in the middle age range where I can view this youth-age tension very dispassionately. However, I did

DEBATES	June 10, 1966
feel some sense of relief when the Prime Minister said there was no upper age limit because, after all, we here do not have very good job security.
This is an impressive move. In some ways it may mark a measure of what might be described as our spiritual maturing, something we have been doing of late in Canada, in that we are concerned to give of our time, our thought and our mental ingenuity to measures like this. This is something which invites and indeed invokes "constructive adventure"-I like that expression of the Prime Minister-on the part of those who are young in years, young in spirit and enthusiastic in endeavour.
The program of the company will provide what we all need, whether we are young, old or middle aged, namely, participation in a meaningful cause, and life is empty indeed if we do not have that. It will also offer opportunities for powerful and purposeful collective activity. We cannot function in isolation; we want to move in groups.
I am impressed and enthusiastic about what has already been done on an interim basis. Since the legislation could not be brought forward when it should have been, it was wise that measures were taken so that valuable and useful time was not lost. The symbol adopted by the company on an interim basis is a most impressive one-the maple key which identifies members of the company, the key which holds the seed for the future. It is a very Canadian symbol, a very meaningful symbol.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In my opinion this deserves great commendation. We are supposed to be a most unimaginative people, we Canadians, but here I think we have shown some real imagination. The seeds will be spread far and wide and I know the returns will be even greater than the beauty of our national emblem. I think too that some of the publications which have been put out by the interim organization should be commended-"better worlds don't just happen, they're made". It continues:
And better worlds are needed-for Canadians in a city slum, on a depressed farm, on an Indian reserve, in a home for the aged.
A better world is needed by people who are poor, under-educated, badly housed; people whose lives open no horizons and whose children have little hope.
This is compelling and appealing. The Company of Young Canadians wants to do something about this world, a world which includes Canada and the developing countries overseas. Now this is only an
June 10, 1966

Idea, but it will be more than an idea when its members go where they have been asked to help, perhaps to a community among the Eskimos or to a slum area where people live eight to a room.
This is an exciting prospect, Mr. Speaker, and I know we all want to accelerate the legislative process of this measure. When we come to the more detailed examination of the legislation we may find things to comment on. I am very impressed with the interim group, but I am sorry there is not a Prince Edward Islander involved. I hope this will be looked after and I have been given the assurance that it will.
These tensions between the generations are not new. Sometimes one reads scare headlines. I have some of them before me. Someone fears a youth rebellion; someone fears a student rebellion. This is not new. Nor is ours the only age where the young have desired and attained leadership. Pitt was prime minister when he was 24. Robespierre was through his bloody and brutal career when 26. Saint-Just had bestrode many of the institutions and too many people and was through at 21. Alexander was very young. Then there was Burns and Mozart. Bonnie Prince Charlie was only 27 when he almost conquered a kingdom which was rightfully his. My colleague reminds me of Robbie Burns whose life gave his fellows great riches and beauty. He was a great benefactor of all mankind and was gone in his thirties.
I am not at all worried. Here I join myself with the views of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). I am not concerned about the inadequacy of the response which the young people of this country will give to what in fact are strenuous and difficult challenges. I say this not because it is a good thing to say of such a measure, nor because it is the kind of easy happy platitude one should drop about such a thing. I have spent most of my life in university classrooms. Since coming here I have formed a close association with the youth sector of our own party. I am greatly buoyed by the fact that I know so well the young people of our particular party, and I am sure we are not unique in that sense. So I speak from knowledge of our young people.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) staked out some areas of tremendous challenge for the company when it becomes fully operative. I believe that many of the members of this house only recently are becoming aware of the needs, challenges and opportunities among the Indian people of
Company of Young Canadians our country. I must confess I have learned a great deal from such members as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the former member for the Northwest Territories, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and various others who have brought to our attention the tremendous compelling needs which exist. Then one thinks of the great vastness to the north and all that can be done, must be done and should be done there. Here in these two areas alone, without moving on to broad horizons in the external field, we have some powerful challenges.
I am glad we have good reason for faith that such a company, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said of young people and young Canadians, can meet. There have been many reasons for making this assertion. Ever so often I hear from some of my former students who are in various parts of the world pushing back the frontiers of ignorance or disease, making magnificent contributions, and revealing the best that Canada has done for them. I do hope as the years go by that the private sector of our society will take a great interest, both in a tangible and intangible way, in this development. As I look at the legislation, which is something which not only legislators but all Canadians should be proud of, I see many opportunities.
Although there is much more I could say, because I want to be brief I will simply end as I began in pledging my complete and thorough-going support for this measure. It is not often one on the opposition side is able so wholeheartedly to endorse what emanates from the other side. I think all of us will look back upon this afternoon as one which in later years we may point to with real pride and deep satisfaction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it is agreed, I should like to make a few remarks before we go into committee. I do not wish to go over again what I think has been stated very well by other hon. members, and that is the enthusiasm with which I think all greet this bill. It is important however that we ask ourselves for a moment why in fact we are doing this. It must seem to some of us at least, when we think about it objectively that we are witnessing here this afternoon a very strange process by which we are giving effect to a bill having to do with an item of interest and concern, primarily never before recognized as part and parcel of government responsibility. Indeed, I must say that what we are doing is much more closely akin to the profession with which I am normally associated, that of the clergy, for it seems to me we are dealing with missionaries and missionary tasks.
I have had to ask myself time and again why it is that governments and government agencies are becoming more and more caught up in human relations, or the development of society in terms of man's relationship with his fellowman. It is fair to say, I think, that in our time we have seen a rapid expansion of interest and concern in this whole area of man's endeavour, and I point out that this is both an exciting and terrifying prospect. Certainly anyone who has read some of what used to be at least avant garde literature such as the writings of Orwell and Huxley about our attempts to design and control man's social relationships, must realize that there would be no future freedoms if we carried this too far.
We must have some expression of concern as to how much in fact we hope, either through direct government intervention or through the establishment of certain crown corporations, to affect the lives of people and the communities in which they live. It must always be the concern of those who represent people in parliaments of the nations, the legislatures of the provinces and councils of the municipalities and townships, to be very sure that when they seek to move into the 
area of human relationships they do not in any way remove from individuals and individual social groups the freedoms that are rightfully theirs.
We must ask ourselves a rhetorical question this afternoon. In our intense anxiety to provide positive and constructive opportunities for young people to participate in nation building or working with the poor, why in fact do we feel called upon to do so? Is it because we are afraid of the restless driving energy of youth, which we are not always sure we can control to our advantage; is it because we feel it is safer to offer opportunities such as these, which may or may not be "safe", or is it, on the other hand, a sign of a failure in our time?
We live in an age of tremendous intercommunication between man, yet in an age in many ways, particularly in our western world, where there seems to be a great lack of confidence in the democratic system and in man's own ability to govern himself responsibly. I would hate to think that we are going to funnel off the vibrant and creative energy of our young people into a number of projects here, there and across the country, and thus deflect the interests of the young people in this country, who primarily must get caught up at some point in the process of governing themselves.
It is somewhat tragic to think of the tremendous cynicism that has developed, particularly among our young people today, regarding the way we govern ourselves, when we are in fact trying to provide opportunities for our youth to participate in this country, not in a democratic process, per se, but through a number of projects which we might assign to them.
These things are all of importance, and I mention them not to paint some dark and gloomy picture of the work that a Company of Young Canadians must do, but so that they can be seen in the context of our Canadian society at the present time. This is not too happy a picture in some ways, but it is a picture which depends to a degree on the objectivity and courage of youth; and if there are weaknesses in the structure of this place and in our system of government it will be not only the wisdom of experience here but the audacity of youth that will change it.
Let us not think that by the creation of a Company of Young Canadians we are going in any sense to offer youth the most important or worth-while role they can play, because in my own mind there may become a
June 10. 1966

much greater role for them in reshaping our country and giving it a new sense of purpose.
Let me now turn to the Company of Young Canadians as such. I can almost stand here this afternoon and say that it was my privilege to be somewhat of a pioneer Young Canadian in the work we attempted to do in Prince Edward Island. We did not have any name for the program as such, but I was fortunate in the parish work I did in Al-berton, Prince Edward Island, to have a parallel vision with both the people resident in that community, and particularly with the local Roman Catholic priest, Father Gerald Steele. We, too, were concerned with many of the things at the local community level that were unhealthy. We were concerned about the lack of educational standards, chronic unemployment, poor home management, lack of recreational facilities for youth and the mobility of only the best people out of the area, with little movement of constructive or helpful people into the area.
One of the things we found as we worked on this project during the past three and a half years was that this was an area in which there was need for great determination and intelligible leadership. Let me say at the outset that when I think of The Company of Young Canadians I am both heartened and disconcerted. I am heartened that there will be very shortly in the field a group of young people willing to wrestle with some of these most difficult problems, but I am very much aware of and disconcerted by the possibility that many of these young people may experience frustrating and disappointing involvements. It is all well and good to offer a program of six weeks training in human relationships to any person, but when it is realized that many of these deep seated social problems can only be dealt with effectively after the two years of service, it will be understood that these young volunteers may suffer terrific frustrations and disappointments.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock.

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that one of the real difficulties of participating in such a program is related to the very nature of the problems involved, because a high degree of frustration and disappointment will be created in almost every case. I am not deterred, nor will I allow myself to be depressed by this fact, for I feel there is enough realism and experience on the part of those who will develop this program that they can create a climate for those who will work in this company in which they will not expect or reach for those achievements which will lead to frustration.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I am concerned, however, in another field. It is one that I am sure will be referred to as we become more and more involved with The Company of Young Canadians. I refer to the calibre of those who will be allowed to participate. It has already been mentioned that the Canadian University Students Overseas, the CUSO program, has offered tremendous opportunities for service overseas for those who have completed or have gone a long way toward completing their university training. However, the fact of the matter is that we have a great number of people who are willing and able to serve, and who I am sure have already submitted applications to The Company of Young Canadians, who will not have this kind of academic background. Indeed, I am sure there will be many instances when academic training and qualifications will not be the prime criteria for effective service.
It has been my good fortune to work with people already in this area of human relationships who have made amazingly significant contributions without necessarily having the academic qualifications that we normally expect. We live in a degree-worshipping generation where, unless you can run a few letters after your name, you are almost not qualified to participate in these more or less esoteric involvements. We must not let our fetish for degrees curb our insight into solving some of these very real problems.
I would hope, too, that when the program gets into high gear it will have a minimum of partisan and political interference. I say this because I think, by its very nature, this
June 10. 1966

Company of Young Canadians program could become the greatest political football in many years. This would be a tragedy, because no generation is more acutely aware of partisan or political influence than youth, and none will become more cynical and despairing of the program than young people being manipulated for this kind of purpose.
It is important for another reason, too, that the program become as independent as it possibly can, because as the Prime Minister said it must have a maximum amount of independence and must be encouraged to be experimental as well as responsible. The very fact that the prime part of this program will move into new and unknown areas will necessitate risks, and it will necessitate our acceptance of the fact that from time to time there will be failure; and it is a well known fact that governments, just like churches, are not prepared very often to accept failure.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that some of the most glorious things that may happen under this program will be, not its successes but its failures, because it will be willing to take the risks in the projects put forward that no other agency or group is willing to take-and that will be all to its credit. We must consider that The Company of Young Canadians may be most responsible when they are taking some of the greatest risks.
It is my conviction that, while it is easy now to say that this may be a program patterned after those of other nations, The Company of Young Canadians may yet have something to offer the young people in our country, namely an opportunity to serve in an exciting and creative way. We seem to be most anxious to praise the programs of other countries, and institutions which put forward this kind of altruistic endeavour; but I am hopeful, both because of the calibre of the men who are connected in the initial stages with this program and because of the general nature of this legislation, that The Company of Young Canadians will offer young people a chance to participate effectively in the development of this nation in the second century of its history.

Mr. Chairman, if I may speak just briefly on this clause I should like to express on behalf of the Prime Minister, who regrettably had to be absent at this time, his appreciation for the quality of co-operation in this very important debate. I know that some hon. members who have spoken could have continued at very much greater length, but certainly the quality of the speeches we have heard today augurs well for this brave new company.
It is my feeling, sir, as a person who is no longer young yet perhaps not really old, that this present generation, this nest of young
June 10. 1966

eagles who from the standpoint of some of us have known only peace and luxury, the children of this affluent society, have insight into social problems both national and international to a degree not evidenced by any of their ancestors. We see in the young people in our high schools and universities a generation which appreciates that mankind does not possess the earth but holds it only in trust. Today we have the opportunity, through this legislation, to establish a corporation for those of them who dare to show their feelings for this nation and for the world.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
We have all kinds of caring. A few days ago I was in my own area, in Smiths Falls, and I visited the Ontario Hospital for Retarded Children. I watched, fascinated, as one small child, with a part of one arm, lovingly fed a less fortunate spastic child spoonfuls of porridge. I was impressed with some of the things I heard from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle about the problems of spastics and other unfortunates. Then, of course, at the very head of our Canadian family we have people like the Vaniers who regard humanity as a family, and life itself as a stewardship and trust. This is an opportunity for our young people, with their time, their talent or their money, to give of themselves more generously than any of us since we, in past generations, have been impelled only to heed the call of country or the world in time of war.
Last night I was looking at a translation of Dag Hammarskj old's "Markings" by Leif Sjoberg. Shortly after his appointment as Secretary General, Hammarskjold wrote for a radio program of Edward R. Murrow the following:
From generations of soldiers and government officials on my father's side I inherited a belief that no life was more satisfactory than one of selfless service to your country

or humanity. This service required a sacrifice of all personal interests, . . .
From scholars and clergymen on my mother's side I inherited a belief that, in the very radical sense of the Gospels, all men were equals as children of God-
Here we have, just before the centennial of our confederation, an opportunity for a generation which sometimes we find frightening in their directness, a generation which believes very much in involvement with mankind, for those who dare to show their feelings for this nation's life, to give themselves to every interest, organization, society and group, its men, women and above all its
Company of Young Canadians children. This is an opportunity for those who conceive of the human race as the only race that matters, and each member thereof as being a part of the family of God. As we move into the study of this bill clause by clause, all of us ought to salute this company of happy warriors.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
No measure announced by the
government during the past three years has been received as warmly as the announcement the government made last year in the Throne Speech indicating its intention to establish The Company of Young Canadians as a vehicle to harness the enthusiasm and imagination of Canadian youth, and of older Canadians who are at least young in spirit. Canadian youth served Canada and the world during the war years in the defence of democracy. Since the war, succeeding generations of Canadian youth have lacked the opportunities for service such as The Company of Young Canadians is going to provide.
Certain cynics have been quick to point out that the C.Y.C. is a Canadian copy of the United States Peace Corps. If any group or body can claim parenthood for the Peace Corps or The Company of Young Canadians I think, as the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out, it is the Christian churches of the world who for centuries have sent missionaries out in the service of others. I am confident that the C.Y C. will remain, in structure, organization and the type of project it will embark upon, strictly Canadian. It will reflect Canadian circumstances, Canadian abilities and Canadian needs. Canada today is in a position to supply teachers, technicians, doctors and nurses to serve in the underdeveloped countries of the world in two major languages.

French Canadians have a particularly significant role to play in Africa, in southeast Asia and in Latin America.
Up to now, the Canadian effort among the new French speaking African nations has been quite inadequate. These people have an urgent need for teachers and technicians to activate their development. Would not the dispatch of such personnel be the ideal way for us to fill the gap and, at the same time, show the interest of our country?
1English1
In its first year of operation, the C.Y.C. has wisely decided to limit itself to projects within Canada. The government has, in the past
June 10. 1966

Company of Young Canadians year, radically expanded its aid to CUSO, the Canadian University Service Overseas. CUSO has developed, over the past few years, into a very successful, privately supported Peace Corps type operation. The government has obviously decided that rather than have C.Y.C. set up a parallel external program, it would work initially through CUSO. I disagree with the hon. member for Red Deer in that I sincerely hope it is not the government's or C.Y.C.'s intention to channel their future external efforts through CUSO. If my opinion is correct, the persons sent to underdeveloped countries through the CUSO program have been teachers, doctors, nurses or medical technicians. In my opinion, we should continue to make use of CUSO in so far as this category of volunteer is concerned, but I would strongly urge the C.Y.C. to branch into the external field in other categories of volunteer work.
I would include amongst these categories, although I certainly do not believe they are absolute, technicians, farmers, engineers and personnel trained in community development work. The most pressing need in the world today is food. With a program designed to attract young Canadian farm people, I am confident that the C.Y.C. could make a contribution to the world's fight against hunger.

However, I do believe that in the presentation of this particular measure this afternoon and in the establishment of this Company of Young Canadians it may somehow or other present to young people another challenging avenue of service that will catch their imagination and give them some purpose and objective in life.
Our generation in this age has been characterized in various ways. It has been characterized as materialistic, thinking only of dollars and cents, losing sight of the intangibles, the human resources and the spiritual factors that make life worth living. It has been characterized as a selfish age in which people are concerned only with themselves and are not thinking of others. It has been characterized as an age of youthful irresponsibility. But I do not believe that these are true characterizations in all respects.
I think the challenge offered by the concept of this Company of Young Canadians is the repudiation of these characteristics and the demonstration of their opposites-the recognition of human values and the needs of those round about us, the challenge of those intangibles that mean so much to our day and to any generation. So that I believe that this is a challenge to the personality of those who will be participating in this program. Those young people and others who accept this challenge and give themselves in service will benefit in the development and enrichment of their own lives.
In addition, as has been pointed out today on a number of occasions, they will assist in an enlarged program of bringing assistance to those who, perhaps, are less fortunate and have not had the similar opportunities for development that others have had. He used to come to area council meetings, and to local union meetings asking for support for the international free trade unions. He encouraged a program of supplying educational facilities and technical facilities to underdeveloped countries, and was trying to

raise money from the people such as I represented in the labour movement-miners and others with no education at all. His concentration always was on the practical advantage that could be provided to the areas he wanted to help. He always managed to gain support for programs similar to those to be undertaken by The Company of Young Canadians. He always said that if the doors are thrown open wide enough, surprising things will come from the most unexpected sources. That is a very broad translation, probably, of a famous statement.
I hope that those charged with the operation of The Company of Young Canadians will keep in mind problems facing children today, particularly of those who do not know what to do at university, and who listen to the teacher saying to them, "This profession is worth a minimum of $20,000 and a maximum of $70,000 a year, and this one is in another minimum and maximum category". These students want to choose a profession, not because they like it, but because it will be a good money producer.
This sort of thing is common in most of our universities, as it is in the teaching profession. I can see a role in The Company of Young Canadians for those young people who have finished high school and who do not know what they want to do. By serving with the company, by being allowed to work with other people, they will be able to learn the needs of other people and at the same time develop in themselves a certain amount of dedication to humanity which will enable them to choose a profession to provide the greatest benefit to the people they will serve, whatever the profession may be.
The benefits accruing from The Company of Young Canadians will be twofold. While benefits will flow to those being served, a great deal of advantage will come to the volunteers, who will learn the needs of other people, and who will thereby develop a certain amount of humility.
Most young people today are products of an affluent society. You give them an allowance, not because they really need it, but because you want to get rid of them. Everybody is too busy to be a boy scout leader to the youth of today. The Company of Young Canadians will develop humility in the volunteers and, as the hon. member for Prince said, will enable those volunteers to grow up and serve in a role that is much needed throughout the world today. Many

Young people today are very suspicious of the generation ahead of them. For this reason I think the government was wise to provide that control of this organization should remain with the young people themselves, so that they might not be overshadowed by their elders telling them to do this, to do that or, what is more likely, not to do this or not to do that.
If The Company of Young Canadians is to be a success it must create a disturbance. It must go into areas of our society where there is darkness, offering a gleam of hope. For too long we have been hearing about ways of improving productivity, increasing our gross national product and making bigger things bigger. We have now reached a stage in our
DEBATES	6281
Company of Young Canadians development where we should think of the inner side of man and consider his spiritual needs, because it is not money alone which satisfies our hopes and desires.
There are many in our society who have not enjoyed the opportunity, to develop as they ought. There has been a great deal of wasted human material. The Company of Young Canadians is an instrument which Canadian society can use to improve the whole of society and give a better chance to those areas which are below our national standards. The company will make a great many mistakes. Many questions will be asked in this house because of those mistakes. But we should realize that it is moving into relatively new fields and we must give it as much scope as possible in order that it may conduct its important experiments.
Above all, I feel The Company of Young Canadians is a challenge to the youth of Canada. They will go through a unique experience as a result of which they will have a wider knowledge of the variety of the human condition. And what is even more important, perhaps they will have a better understanding of themselves and of the society in which they live.
There will be problems. There will be set-backs. At times these volunteers will be very depressed. But as it is said, we learn very little from success in comparison with what we learn in defeat. I wish these volunteers well as they go out on this noble experiment. I hope they will consider themselves as people who are setting out to improve the lives and the physical conditions of others. It is not in material possessions that true happiness is to be found. Volunteers must have faith, and faith requires a great deal of courage. It consists of the ability to take a risk-a readiness to accept pain and disappointment. Whoever in the company insists on safety and security as a primary condition of an operation will be a failure. Ministers directed the Permanent Representatives to continue to examine closely the prospects of healthy developments in East-West relations, and to prepare a full report on these questions for meetings to be attended, as far as is practicable, by the Foreign Ministers of the various countries. This report, which should deal with all possible initiatives in this field, would cover, inter alia, problems connected with European security and German reunification.
12.	Ministers expressed their continuous interest in progress towards general, complete and controlled disarmament. They expressed great concern over the problem of nuclear proliferation in its world-wide implications and their determination to continue their efforts to solve this problem. In particular, the governments concerned in the 18-Power Geneva Conference reaffirmed their intention to do their utmost to achieve positive results.
13.	With regard to Greek-Turkish relations, Ministers took note of the Secretary General's report on the "Watching Brief" and confirmed their support for the continuation of his activities in this respect. They welcomed the announcement made by the Foreign Ministers of Greece and Turkey to the effect that "the Governments of Greece and Turkey, inspired by a sincere desire to facilitate a peaceful and agreed solution of the Cyprus problem and to improve their relations, have decided to proceed to contacts and exchanges of views on the Cyprus question and on Greek-Turkish relations. The procedure to be followed during these contacts will be decided in common". The ministers reiterated their appreciation of the continued presence of the United Nations Force in Cyprus and expressed their support of the efforts of the United Nations for safeguarding peace and improving the situation in the island.
14.	Ministers reaffirmed their desire to promote economic co-operation in the spirit of Article 2 of the North Atlantic Treaty. They acknowledged the need to join efforts in order to promote research in the scientific, technical and production fields, and achieve a wider co-operation and exchange of information so that in a world of rapid scientific progress the gap in technological achievement between Europe and North America can be narrowed.

June 10, 1966
15.	All economically advanced countries, those of East and West alike, have a common responsibility to co-operate in attacking the fundamental problems confronting the developing countries. Progress toward political settlements and disarmament will contribute to this end by releasing resources and energies which are so badly needed for the advancement of human welfare.
16.	The Council, agreeing that efforts should be continued to supply Greece and Turkey with defence assistance within the framework of the Alliance, in order to help them maintain an effective contribution to the common defence, adopted a resolution recommending wider participation in this aid programme.
17.	Ministers received a progress report on the activities of the Special Committee of Defence Ministers which was created by the
Council in 1965. A further report will be submitted to the Council during the Ministerial session in December.
18.	In view of the importance of science and technology to the military strength of the Alliance and the economic vitality of its members, Ministers noted with satisfaction the recently agreed improvements in procedures for co-operation among members of the Alliance in research, development and production of military equipment. They encouraged member countries to bring suitable projects forward for co-operative action.
19.	They noted that a meeting of Defence Ministers will be convened in July to review and carry forward the institution of Force Planning procedures for projecting and adjusting annually a five-year program.
20.	A meeting of the Council at Ministerial level will be held in December 1966.
